questions.question: Explain why the design process requires two possible solutions, what makes two ideas genuinely different, and why the sketches at this stage are drawn free-hand.
questions.expected_answer: Two ideas are required because a team's first idea is rarely its best and a second idea developed with equal care gives a real comparison rather than a formality. Genuinely different ideas take different routes or address different life-cycle stages, such as a container of a new material versus a returnable deposit-backed container or a collection crate, whereas two sizes or colours of the same object are one idea. Sketches are free-hand because at the idea stage the drawing must keep pace with thinking, instruments slow the hand and force premature commitment to dimensions, and a rough sketch invites criticism and change where a ruled drawing looks finished; instrument drawings follow after the choice.

questions.question: Describe the techniques that make a free-hand sketch readable, including the use of exploded and cut-away views, and list what must be annotated.
questions.expected_answer: Begin with faint construction lines or a box to fix proportions, then draw the outline more firmly; draw a rough three-dimensional view so depth is visible and add small secondary views where the main view hides a feature. An exploded view separates the parts along their assembly line to show how they fit, such as a lid floating above its box; a cut-away or section slices the object to show the inside, such as a double wall or stiffening rib; a detail enlarges a small feature. Annotate every part with its name, its material and thickness, approximate overall dimensions, the forces acting and how they are resisted, how the user handles, cleans or disposes of it, and how it reduces the harm in the brief, with arrows linking notes to parts; shading is light and least important.

questions.question: Describe how two sketched ideas are compared against the brief, using the taxi-rank example, and explain what happens to the rejected idea.
questions.expected_answer: A table lists the specifications and constraints down the side and the two ideas across the top, each cell recording met, partly met or not met with a brief reason. For the taxi rank, the paperboard container probably holds a hot meal for 30 minutes pending a test, stacks twenty high with a ribbed base, costs about forty cents more, breaks down within a year, needs no bins or water and is likely to be accepted; the returnable container holds and stacks well and is cheap per meal if returned often, is not thrown away if the deposit works, but needs a return point and washing water the rank lacks and depends on uncertain customer behaviour. The team chooses with written reasons, borrows useful features from the losing idea such as a return crate for composting, and keeps the rejected sketch in the portfolio as evidence of the comparison and a source of ideas.
